paragraphs: Verification asks whether examples belong to the same class, including classes absent from training. This makes the comparison rule especially important: useful representations must support decisions about unfamiliar categories. The paper learns both an encoder and a parameterized, distance-like comparison function together, rather than relying on a fixed comparison score after learning representations.

The learned pseudo-distance also has statistical interpretations. The authors show that its output approximates a likelihood ratio, allowing it to support hypothesis tests about whether examples share a class. They additionally connect the model to a large divergence between the joint distributions of same-class and different-class pairs. These interpretations explain how the learned comparison separates the two verification cases.

In empirical evaluations, the approach improves on simple scorers such as cosine similarity and on widely used downstream classifiers. Training is also reported to be simpler than metric learning with actual distances, without requiring complex pair-harvesting schemes. The contribution combines a learned verification rule, statistical interpretations, and a simpler training procedure.
icml-2020-an-end-to-end-approach-for-the.tldr: Jointly learning an encoder and a distance-like comparison function improves verification of unfamiliar classes and simplifies training in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Self-supervised visual learning trains a feature extractor using a task whose labels can be generated without human annotation. A problem arises when that task can be solved through superficial clues, such as watermarks or color aberrations. Success on the training task can then fail to produce representations that capture useful semantic information.

The paper proposes an automatic way to reduce these shortcuts. Its central assumption is that features exploited early in training may also be especially vulnerable to an adversary that makes the task harder. A separate lens network learns small image modifications chosen to maximally reduce performance on the pretext task. Training on the altered images therefore challenges the features supporting an easy solution.

Across the common pretext tasks and datasets tested, the authors find support for this assumption. Representations trained with lens-modified images outperform those trained without them in every tested case. The modifications also provide insight into which features different tasks and datasets encourage, making the lens both a training intervention and a way to inspect shortcut learning.
icml-2020-automatic-shortcut-removal-for.tldr: An adversarial lens network makes small image changes that discourage shortcuts and improve self-supervised representations across the tested settings.

paragraphs: A neural classifier can make a prediction with high confidence even when it is wrong. This creates problems when confidence helps determine whether a prediction should be trusted. The paper addresses the issue through training, aiming to make the class probabilities already produced by a network more useful as confidence estimates.

The proposed Correctness Ranking Loss regularizes those probabilities so that confidence has a better ordinal relationship with correctness. The emphasis is on ordering predictions by confidence: predictions that deserve more trust should receive higher confidence scores. This ranking objective is the specific property studied, rather than a claim that every probability becomes an exact measure of correctness.

The method works with existing architectures without modification, has almost the training cost of conventional deep classifiers, and requires only one inference pass. Classification experiments indicate improved confidence rankings. The authors also demonstrate benefits for out-of-distribution detection and active learning, showing that better confidence ordering can help tasks that use uncertainty to guide decisions.
icml-2020-confidence-aware-learning-for-.tldr: Correctness Ranking Loss trains existing classifiers to produce better-ordered confidence estimates with little additional computational cost.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning system must decide both what action to take and how often it can change that action. The paper studies this second choice through action persistence: repeating an action for a fixed number of decision steps. Changing persistence changes the effective control frequency and can affect the quality of the policy that learning produces.

The authors first analyze how persistence changes the performance of the optimal policy. They then introduce Persistent Fitted Q-Iteration, or PFQI, an extension of Fitted Q-Iteration designed to learn the optimal value function for a specified persistence. This gives the control-frequency choice an explicit place in the learning procedure.

The paper provides a theoretical study of PFQI and a heuristic for selecting persistence. Benchmark experiments demonstrate advantages from action persistence and support the effectiveness of the selection method. These results suggest that control frequency deserves attention as part of policy learning, while the persistence-selection procedure remains a heuristic rather than a stated guarantee of finding the best setting.
icml-2020-control-frequency-adaptation-v.tldr: PFQI incorporates repeated actions into batch reinforcement learning, with theory and experiments showing the value of choosing control frequency carefully.

paragraphs: Training on a smaller dataset saves work only if the selected examples still support a good solution. This paper introduces CRAIG, which chooses a weighted subset of training examples, called a coreset. Its selection criterion aims to make the subset closely approximate the gradient of the full dataset, preserving the information used to update the model.

CRAIG constructs this subset by maximizing a submodular function. For convex optimization, the authors prove that incremental gradient methods applied to the subset converge to an optimal or near-optimal solution at the same convergence rate as the corresponding full-data method. The resulting speedup scales inversely with subset size, connecting reduced data processing to the optimization guarantee.

Experiments extend the practical investigation to logistic regression and deep neural networks. CRAIG reaches practically the same solution while accelerating incremental gradient methods by up to six times for logistic regression and three times for neural networks. The convex convergence theorem and the neural-network experiments provide distinct forms of support for the approach.
icml-2020-coresets-for-data-efficient-tr.tldr: CRAIG selects weighted training subsets that approximate full-data gradients, offering convex convergence guarantees and substantial measured training speedups.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn halfspaces, classifiers that separate inputs using a linear boundary, when an adversary can perturb the inputs. Robust learning must account for those allowed changes when finding a classifier. The setting is distribution-independent, so the investigation does not rely on choosing a particular input distribution.

The first result addresses the realizable setting, where the learning problem admits a suitable classifier. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions on the adversarial perturbation sets for efficient robust learning of halfspaces. This characterizes which permitted changes allow an efficient solution in that setting. Both directions matter: the conditions establish when learning is possible and identify requirements for that possibility.

The second result introduces random label noise, so the observed labels can be corrupted. For this case, the authors provide a simple, computationally efficient algorithm covering any perturbation defined by an ℓp norm. Together, the results address both the structure of allowable adversarial changes and the additional challenge of unreliable labels.
icml-2020-efficiently-learning-adversari.tldr: The paper characterizes efficient robust learning of halfspaces in the realizable setting and gives an efficient algorithm for ℓp perturbations with random label noise.

paragraphs: Clustering can produce assignments that are difficult to explain because many features interact in determining membership. This paper studies partitions represented by small decision trees, whose decisions provide straightforward descriptions of clusters. It measures the quality of these explainable partitions using the usual k-means and k-medians objectives.

The theoretical results show that interpretability can carry a cost. Popular top-down tree-building methods can produce arbitrarily expensive clusterings. More fundamentally, a worst-case approximation penalty of at least order log k is unavoidable for clustering represented by a tree with k leaves. This lower bound identifies a limitation of the tree representation itself, beyond the shortcomings of particular construction methods.

The authors also provide positive guarantees. For two clusters, a single threshold achieves a constant-factor approximation, with nearly matching lower bounds. For larger k, an efficient algorithm gives O(k) approximation for k-medians and O(k²) for k-means. These guarantees do not depend on data dimension or input size, making the quality-versus-explainability tradeoff mathematically explicit.
icml-2020-explainable-k-means-and-k-medi.tldr: Small decision trees make clusters explainable, and this paper bounds both their unavoidable clustering cost and the quality achievable by efficient algorithms.

paragraphs: Learning non-discriminatory predictors can require information about protected attributes, yet sensitive demographic data may be unavailable because its collection is restricted. The paper addresses the tension between keeping this information private and making it useful for fair learning. Its starting point is a scheme through which individuals release sensitive information in a privatized form.

The authors then show how to adapt non-discriminatory learning methods to use these privatized attributes. This matters because releasing a private version of an attribute does not by itself establish that a downstream learning procedure can use it effectively. The paper supplies theoretical performance guarantees for the adapted learners, connecting the release scheme to the resulting prediction task.

The framework allows downstream entities to learn from the privatized information rather than requiring direct access to the original attributes. The authors also discuss how the methodology could extend to cases where protected attributes exist for only part of the dataset. That partial-data application is presented as a possible use of the methodology.
icml-2020-fair-learning-with-private-dem.tldr: The paper combines private release of sensitive attributes with adapted fair-learning methods that have theoretical performance guarantees.

paragraphs: An environment can generate an enormous variety of observations while having a much smaller underlying state space. HOMER addresses reinforcement learning in environments that admit such an unknown latent-state description. Its aim is to make exploration depend on the underlying structure rather than on the sheer number of possible observations.

The algorithm alternates between learning a representation, called a kinematic state abstraction, and using that representation to explore strategically. Newly learned abstractions help it reach new states, connecting representation learning directly to exploration. The authors prove that its sample complexity grows polynomially with the number of latent states and the time horizon, without depending on observation-space size, even when that space is infinite.

The exploration guarantee also supports sample-efficient global policy optimization for any reward function in this setting. Efficient implementation is conditional on the tractability of certain supervised learning problems. In a challenging exploration experiment, HOMER uses samples more efficiently than standard reinforcement learning baselines, providing empirical support alongside its theoretical guarantees.
icml-2020-kinematic-state-abstraction-an.tldr: HOMER combines learned state abstractions with exploration, achieving sample guarantees independent of observation-space size under the paper’s latent-state setting.

paragraphs: Neural Theorem Provers combine learned representations with rule-based reasoning and can give logical explanations for predictions. Their computational burden comes from considering every possible proof path for a goal. As the reasoning problem grows, this broad search restricts their usefulness for large-scale applications.

The paper introduces Conditional Theorem Provers, which extend this framework by learning a rule-selection strategy through gradient-based optimization. Reasoning strategy becomes part of what the system learns from data. This addresses the search burden while retaining the combination of neural learning and explainable logical reasoning that motivates the original approach.

The authors report scalability and state-of-the-art results on CLUTRR, a dataset that tests whether learning to reason on smaller graphs transfers to larger ones. They also find improved link-prediction performance over other neural-symbolic models on standard benchmarks, while preserving explainability. These results support learned rule selection as a way to improve both computational practicality and reasoning performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2020-learning-reasoning-strategies-.tldr: Conditional Theorem Provers learn which rules to select, improving scalability and benchmark performance while retaining logical explanations.

paragraphs: Perception draws on incoming observations and on expectations formed from experience and short-term memory. The useful balance between these bottom-up and top-down signals depends on the task and context. The paper explores recurrent neural networks that learn to combine them dynamically, addressing the difficulty of managing many interacting information sources.

The proposed architectures use attention to control how bottom-up and top-down signals are combined. They also divide computation into modules that restrict information sharing. Attention and modularity therefore work together to direct communication, giving the architecture mechanisms for selecting relevant signals instead of allowing all available information to mix freely.

Experiments cover language modeling, sequential image classification, video prediction, and reinforcement learning. The authors report reliable performance improvements on perceptual and language tasks, particularly in robustness to distractions and noisy data. Across the evaluated benchmarks, bidirectional information flow can improve on strong baselines. The findings support controlled, context-sensitive communication as a practical architectural choice without claiming to settle the general question of optimal signal combination.
icml-2020-learning-to-combine-top-down-a.tldr: Attention and modularity help recurrent networks combine observations with expectations, improving performance and robustness across the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Predicting future events becomes difficult when many event types are possible, because an unrestricted neural model may learn accidental patterns. This paper incorporates domain knowledge through a temporal deductive database. Logical rules specify how facts follow from other facts and past events, providing structure for the prediction model.

Each fact carries a changing vector state computed by a neural network. The network’s topology follows the fact’s provenance: the facts and event history that established it. Special facts determine which event types are currently possible, and neural components model their probabilities alongside their states. Logical specification therefore shapes both what can happen and how relevant history enters the prediction.

The authors derive these probabilistic models from concise Datalog programs and evaluate them in synthetic and real-world domains. Encoding appropriate domain knowledge in the architecture improves prediction in those evaluations. The contribution is a way to connect explicit rules about temporal relationships with learned numerical states, allowing the rules to guide the structure of a neural event model.
icml-2020-neural-datalog-through-time-in.tldr: Temporal Datalog rules shape neural event-prediction models, improving predictions by incorporating appropriate domain knowledge into their architecture.

paragraphs: Thompson sampling has strong theoretical and practical performance in multi-armed bandit problems, but each decision requires sampling from a posterior distribution. Repeating that computation can make the method difficult to deploy. Approximate sampling is a practical response, yet its approximation error must be accounted for when establishing guarantees about the decisions it produces.

The paper develops two efficient Langevin Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms specifically for Thompson sampling. The resulting methods use approximate posterior samples while retaining a provable optimal instance-dependent regret guarantee for the bandit problem. Regret describes the loss from choosing actions instead of consistently choosing the best one; instance-dependent analysis reflects the particular problem being solved.

The proof develops new bounds on posterior concentration and on how quickly the sampling procedures converge for log-concave distributions. These results connect the quality of approximate sampling to the quality of sequential decisions. The contribution therefore addresses computational implementation and statistical guarantees together, rather than treating approximate posterior sampling as an unexamined substitute.
icml-2020-on-approximate-thompson-sampli.tldr: Two Langevin sampling algorithms make approximate Thompson sampling efficiently implementable while preserving optimal instance-dependent regret guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly softmax policy-gradient methods converge in the tabular setting, using the true gradient. For the unregularized method, it establishes an O(1/t) convergence rate, where t counts optimization steps. The constants depend on the problem and initialization, making the result more informative than an assurance of eventual convergence alone.

The analysis uses a Łojasiewicz inequality, which relates optimization progress to gradient information. It also bounds the minimum probability assigned to an optimal action during training in terms of its initial probability. These findings help explain why the method can continue moving toward an optimal policy despite the structure of the softmax parameterization.

With entropy regularization, the authors prove a faster O(e⁻ᵗ) rate toward the softmax optimal policy. Additional Ω(1/t) lower bounds help establish the separation between the rates. The results explain how entropy changes policy optimization even when gradients are exact, with non-uniform Łojasiewicz degree providing a further mathematical account of the difference.
icml-2020-on-the-global-convergence-rate.tldr: For tabular softmax policy gradients with exact gradients, the paper proves O(1/t) convergence without entropy and a faster exponential rate toward the entropy-regularized optimum.

paragraphs: A recommendation affects more than the user receiving it. When content providers need a minimum level of engagement to remain viable, today’s recommendations influence which providers will be available later. This paper studies that coupling between users and providers, treating long-term utility as a property of the recommendation ecosystem.

The authors formulate the task as selecting an equilibrium of a dynamical system and show that it can be solved through optimal constrained matching. Within their model, the selected equilibrium maximizes social welfare while supporting a sufficiently diverse collection of viable providers. The matching constraints make provider survival part of the recommendation objective.

Even in a simple, stylized model, always matching each user to their currently best provider performs poorly. The paper develops scalable techniques for solving the constrained matching problem and connects the outcomes to user regret and fairness. Its fairness argument is utilitarian: it concerns aggregate welfare. The results show why immediate individual utility can be an inadequate guide to long-term recommendation quality.
icml-2020-optimizing-long-term-social-we.tldr: Constrained matching accounts for provider viability to maximize long-term social welfare in the paper’s recommendation-system model.

paragraphs: Learning user preferences becomes challenging when choices occupy a high-dimensional space and the objective cannot be measured directly. This paper proposes a Bayesian optimization framework built around a different form of feedback. Its central assumption is that a user can identify a minimizer along a projection, even though the full objective value is unavailable.

The authors call this interaction a projective preferential query. It asks for an optimal choice within the queried projection, supplying a structured preference signal for optimization. The query is designed to support natural human interaction. A user experiment demonstrates this with feedback about the preferred position and orientation of a molecule adsorbing to a surface.

The paper demonstrates that the framework can find a global minimum of a high-dimensional black-box function in a task described as infeasible for existing pairwise-comparison preference methods. This is a demonstrated capability under the proposed feedback model. Its significance lies in changing the information requested from users so that preference-based optimization can handle the evaluated high-dimensional search.
icml-2020-projective-preferential-bayesi.tldr: Projective preference queries let users guide high-dimensional Bayesian optimization by identifying an optimum along a projection.

paragraphs: Preconditioning changes how a gradient-based optimizer turns gradient information into parameter updates. A block-diagonal preconditioner divides coordinates into groups, allowing update computations for different groups to run as independent parallel tasks. This paper asks whether those groups should remain fixed throughout optimization.

The proposed technique randomly repartitions coordinates across tasks as optimization proceeds. Each update retains the block structure that supports parallel computation, while the assignment of coordinates to blocks changes. The authors show that this randomization can substantially improve convergence and provide a theoretical analysis characterizing the expected gains from repartitioning.

Experiments on several traditional machine learning tasks validate the theoretical findings. The implementation argument is especially favorable when shared memory is available: randomization can then be added efficiently to existing methods. The contribution makes the partition itself an active part of optimization design, showing how a structure chosen for parallel execution can be adjusted during learning to improve convergence.
icml-2020-randomized-block-diagonal-prec.tldr: Randomly repartitioning coordinates improves the expected convergence of block-diagonal preconditioned optimization while retaining parallel update structure.

paragraphs: System identification learns a dynamical model from observations, supporting control, state estimation, and prediction. This paper considers offline identification of nonlinear systems whose full state is not observed. It investigates certainty-equivalent expectation-maximization as a scalable approach for high-dimensional deterministic systems, a setting relevant to robotics.

The authors formulate the method as block coordinate ascent and provide an efficient implementation. Their evidence for reliability and scalability is empirical. On a simulated system of coupled Lorenz attractors, the algorithm identifies high-dimensional dynamics in settings that can be intractable for particle-based approaches. This experiment addresses a computational obstacle associated with representing unobserved system behavior.

The method is also applied to an aerobatic helicopter. By adding unobserved fluid states to the model, the authors learn dynamics that predict helicopter acceleration better than state-of-the-art approaches in their evaluation. Together, the examples support certainty-equivalent EM as a practical identification method for the studied systems, including cases where useful state variables are hidden from direct observation.
icml-2020-scalable-identification-of-par.tldr: An efficient certainty-equivalent EM implementation empirically scales to high-dimensional hidden-state dynamics and improves helicopter acceleration prediction.

paragraphs: People may change their behavior in response to a classifier that makes consequential decisions about them. Such adaptation can improve a desired quality, or it can merely improve the chance of receiving a favorable decision. This paper develops a causal framework that distinguishes these two possibilities in strategic classification.

Existing approaches often describe adaptation through a cost function that determines which changes are rational for an individual. The authors show that encouraging genuine improvement involves a deeper requirement: any procedure that designs classifiers with such incentives must solve a non-trivial causal inference problem. The result identifies causal reasoning as a necessary component of that design task.

A related theorem applies to constructing cost functions that satisfy requirements used in previous work. Thus, specifying how difficult changes are does not remove the underlying causal challenge. The contribution explains why designing incentives requires understanding how behavioral changes affect the desired outcome, and reveals causal modeling assumptions within approaches previously framed primarily as strategic classification.
icml-2020-strategic-classification-is-ca.tldr: The paper proves that designing classifiers to incentivize genuine improvement necessarily entails a non-trivial causal inference problem.

paragraphs: A strong benchmark score can leave two questions unresolved: whether repeated use has encouraged overfitting to the test set, and whether the model works on different kinds of text. This paper separates those questions by constructing four new test sets for SQuAD question-answering systems.

One test set uses Wikipedia, matching the original domain. Despite extensive reuse of the original test set, the authors find no evidence of adaptive overfitting. The other sets use New York Times articles, Reddit posts, and Amazon product reviews. Across a broad collection of models, average performance falls by 3.8, 14.0, and 17.4 F1 points, respectively, on those domains.

A strong human baseline matches or exceeds model performance in the original domain and shows little or no decline on the new domains. This contrast indicates that the observed model drops are not mirrored by comparable human deterioration. The results support the resilience of holdout evaluation in the studied setting while motivating evaluations that explicitly measure robustness to natural changes in data.
icml-2020-the-effect-of-natural-distribu.tldr: New SQuAD tests find no evidence of adaptive test-set overfitting but substantial model performance drops across naturally different text domains.

paragraphs: The paper studies classification when data come from two high-dimensional Gaussian clusters that overlap enough to create unavoidable errors. Even an oracle that knows the cluster centers misclassifies a small but nonzero fraction of points. This provides a noisy setting in which to examine how regularization affects generalization.

The authors rigorously analyze regularized convex classifiers, including ridge, hinge, and logistic regression. Their analysis takes a high-dimensional limit: both sample count and dimension grow without bound while their ratio remains fixed. This scaling keeps the amount of data relative to the number of dimensions central to the characterization of prediction error.

The results reveal that regularization can, in some cases, bring these classifiers to Bayes-optimal performance, the best achievable for the underlying prediction problem. The paper also illustrates an interpolation peak under weak regularization and examines the effect of unequal cluster sizes. These findings clarify how regularization, dimensionality, and class proportions interact within this specific noisy Gaussian model.
icml-2020-the-role-of-regularization-in-.tldr: A rigorous high-dimensional analysis shows how regularization affects Gaussian-mixture classification and can sometimes achieve Bayes-optimal performance.

paragraphs: An autoencoder learns a compressed representation from which it reconstructs its input. This paper adds an explicit objective for preserving the topology of the input space in that representation. The aim is to retain information about how data are connected across multiple scales while maintaining good reconstruction.

The method uses persistent homology, a tool from topological data analysis, to compute signatures of both the original data and their latent representations. These signatures define a topological loss term. Under weak theoretical assumptions, the authors construct this loss so that it is differentiable, allowing the encoding to learn from the topology-preservation objective.

The authors provide theoretical support and evaluate the approach on a synthetic manifold and real-world image datasets. They report favorable latent representations while keeping reconstruction errors low. The findings support using topology as a trainable representation objective: the compressed space can be encouraged to retain multi-scale connectivity information while still serving the autoencoder’s reconstruction task.
icml-2020-topological-autoencoders-43a84.tldr: A differentiable loss based on persistent homology encourages autoencoders to preserve multi-scale connectivity while maintaining low reconstruction error.

paragraphs: Binary neural networks use weights with two possible values, making them computationally efficient and attractive for hardware. Training is difficult because those discrete choices do not fit ordinary gradient optimization directly. Nevertheless, gradient-based approximations such as the Straight-Through Estimator work well in practice, raising the question of how to justify their design.

The paper applies the Bayesian learning rule to estimate a Bernoulli distribution over the binary weights. This produces a training algorithm that gives a principled explanation for some choices made by earlier approaches. Working with distributions over weights also provides a route to representing uncertainty within the same framework.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and show that the algorithm enables uncertainty estimation and continual learning aimed at avoiding catastrophic forgetting. That extends the role of the method beyond finding a single set of binary weights. The contribution links practical binary-network training techniques to a Bayesian formulation that both explains existing choices and supports additional learning capabilities.
icml-2020-training-binary-neural-network.tldr: A Bayesian rule for learning distributions over binary weights justifies existing training choices and enables uncertainty estimation and continual learning.

paragraphs: Recurrent neural networks usually describe time through successive discrete updates. This formulation is convenient for learning from data because efficient inference methods are available and training need not numerically integrate differential equations. However, continuous-time descriptions can make the mathematical analysis of learned dynamics more convenient and reveal additional insights.

The paper develops a translation from discrete time to continuous time for a particular class of ReLU-based recurrent networks. It proves three theorems establishing mathematical equivalence between the two formulations under different conditions. The scope is therefore a specified network class with conditional equivalence results, rather than an unrestricted conversion of every recurrent architecture.

Examples from machine learning and nonlinear dynamical systems illustrate how the results can be used. The approach connects the practical advantages of fitting discrete-time models with the analytical advantages of continuous-time descriptions. Its central contribution is a mathematical bridge that lets a learned system be examined in another time formulation when the relevant theorem’s conditions are satisfied.
icml-2020-transformation-of-relu-based-r.tldr: Three conditional equivalence theorems translate a particular class of discrete-time ReLU recurrent networks into continuous-time dynamical systems.

paragraphs: Many neural image-processing solutions are designed for a single problem. OneNet offers a more reusable approach by placing a neural network inside an ADMM optimization solver as a proximal operator. This paper extends that framework to video and makes two components suitable for end-to-end learning through backpropagation.

First, the authors add bidirectional recurrent connections to the convolutional prior network, allowing its processing to incorporate temporal information in both directions. Second, they replace the fixed linear data step with a trainable bidirectional convolutional recurrent network. The changes bring learned video processing into both the prior component and the solver’s data step.

Experiments on Rotated MNIST, Scanned CIFAR-10, and UCF-101 cover tasks including inpainting, super resolution, deblurring, frame interpolation, prediction, and colorization. The modifications substantially improve performance over end-to-end convolutional OneNet and 3D Wavelet sparsity in the reported experiments. The two changes are complementary, with their combination producing the best results, supporting the value of adapting both solver components to video.
icml-2020-videoonenet-bidirectional-conv.tldr: VideoOneNet adds bidirectional recurrence and a trainable data step to OneNet, producing complementary improvements across multiple video-processing tasks.
